label: b46: c51 at n=4 -- batch 512, soft target, 21 / 201 atoms, one config a wave (vs b38)
notes:
THIS WAVE: 51 atoms -> 201, over the same support [-5, 120]. Atom spacing goes 2.50 -> 0.625. Four arms,
seeds 1-4, each paired against b38d-c51fc320eps3125seed4.

WHY IT IS LAST, AND IT HAS THE WEAKEST PRIOR OF THE FOUR. This is the other bracket around 51, included
so the resolution question has an answer in both directions rather than a one-sided null -- but the prior
is against it, for the same reason b46a's prior is for it: 4x the atoms is 4x the output-layer parameters
estimated from the same data, so if c51's problem is a noisy loss this makes it worse. What argues for
running it is the specific shape of this domain's value function. Returns cluster tightly near a win, and
the difference between a board that will be filled and one that will not is small in value terms; at 2.50
per atom that distinction may fall inside a single bin, in which case the head literally cannot represent
it and finer atoms are not a luxury but the fix. Last position also makes it the free wave to cancel if
the schedule binds.

THE ALTERNATIVE THAT WAS CONSIDERED AND NOT TAKEN. C51_DOUBLE=0 was the other candidate for this slot and
is better-motivated on paper -- double-Q's action selection interacts with a categorical head in a way
nothing here has isolated. It was left out only to keep the batch to one theme per pair (a/b = the loss
and its target, c/d = the support's resolution), so a two-sided null on c and d closes the resolution
question cleanly. IF c AND d BOTH COME BACK NULL AT n=4, C51_DOUBLE=0 IS THE NEXT BATCH, not a third atom
count.

READINGS. (1) Better -- the support was under-resolved near the top, the most interesting result
available here, because it points at the reward scale rather than at c51. Follow up by checking whether a
NARROWER support at 51 atoms buys the same thing more cheaply, since that is finer resolution without the
parameter cost. (2) Null -- expected. (3) Worse, and worse while b46a is better, would be the strongest
possible evidence for the noisy-loss story: more atoms hurt, more data per atom helped, same axis,
opposite signs.

THE BATCH, AND ITS SHAPE. Four one-knob variants of b38's c51 config, each run on ALL FOUR of b38's
seeds -- 16 arms, 3M steps each, four at a time. Everything else is b38's config verbatim, so every arm
has a SEED-MATCHED control in b38 and the batch is a PAIRED comparison rather than two group means.
That is the whole reason for the shape: b38's own four arms pooled 78.51 / 71.79 / 72.53 / 72.66, a 6.7
pp spread at n=1, so a single unpaired arm cannot see anything smaller than its own seed. Pairing
removes that variance instead of averaging over it, and it is why seeds 1-4 were reused rather than
fresh ones -- a fresh seed would have no control to pair with.

ONE CONFIG PER WAVE, SEEDS 1-4 TOGETHER. Priorities are 30 / 31 / 32 / 33 for b46a / b46b / b46c /
b46d, and the daemon's wave barrier takes the four lowest-priority jobs and starts nothing new until
all four finish -- so each wave is exactly one config at n=4 and every wave produces a COMPLETE,
readable answer about one knob. Nothing has to be held back for a later wave to become interpretable,
which is the point: a wave can be read and acted on the day it lands, and the batch can be stopped
after any wave without leaving a half-measured config behind.

BUDGET ~3 DAYS OF WALL CLOCK, and the first wave is the slowest. 16 arms at 3M with 4 trainer slots is
four sequential waves plus a close-out each. b46a is ~4x the backward-pass FLOPs of the others, so wave
1 is the long one; the remaining three should run at roughly b38's speed. If the schedule binds, b46d
(201 atoms) is the wave to cut -- weakest prior of the four, for exactly the reason b46a has the
strongest -- and because it is last, cutting it costs nothing already spent.

WHY b38 AND NOT b36 IS THE BASELINE. The two differ only in Adam epsilon (b36 1.5e-4, b38 3.125e-4)
and that dose is closed: sign test p = 0.625, no effect. b38 is also the batch that ran to the full
3.00M on all four arms, while b36 was stopped at 1.87-2.02M -- so at the 3M horizon these arms are
capped at, b38 is the only exact 4-seed control that exists. Choosing it costs nothing and buys a real
baseline.

WHAT THE WHOLE BATCH IS ABOUT. c51 has underperformed the scalar arms across b36/b38 and the suspicion
is that the shortfall is in the LOSS, not the algorithm: a categorical head learns a distribution over
51 atoms from the same single transition a scalar head uses for one number, and the projected Bellman
target is rebuilt from a target network that jumps discontinuously across the whole support every 1000
steps. Waves a and b attack the gradient's noise and the target's smoothness; c and d bracket 51 atoms
to ask whether the resolution is wrong in either direction. Every c51 arm in this project has run
BATCH_SIZE=128 and TARGET_UPDATE_PERIOD=1000 -- both DQN defaults, neither chosen for a distributional
loss. If all four waves come back null, the shortfall is not in these knobs and the next places to look
are the priority signal (kl vs ce) and C51_DOUBLE.

HOW TO JUDGE A WAVE. Per-seed differences against the matched b38 arm, then a sign test across the four
seeds -- the same reading the b42-b45 ladder used, where 4-of-4 at a mean of +2.0 pp was the result that
closed a rung. Even at n=4 this project cannot resolve an effect below ~10 pp on score alone, so churn
(perDiagnostics/c51_stability.py) is the primary signal and score is the confirmation; churn resolved a
~4x effect on a pair where n=2 score could not. DO NOT read peak_trailing -- it is trailing average
SCORE, saturated at 95/95 for anything that fills a board.

NOT A HOF ATTEMPT. 3M from scratch does not reach the >=98% band, so expect auto_hof to exit `done` with
nothing measured on every arm. That is normal, not a failure.

MEASUREMENT ERA. These are batch-45-onward arms: graph evals are 20 episodes, so perfect_percent comes
in multiples of 5 rather than 10. best_perfect30 and max_single_eval are maxima over a noisy statistic
and are biased DOWN relative to b36/b38's 10-episode era -- do not compare those two metrics across the
boundary. The bias is IDENTICAL for all sixteen arms, so it cancels within the batch and only distorts
the comparison to b38; prefer banded means or the close-out for that. The close-out runs on the
vectorised engine, which is flat and ungated (min_achievable: null), so its rows are directly poolable;
b38's rows were gated at 95.

EACH WAVE GETS ONE CLOSE-OUT COVERING ITS FOUR SEEDS, and for waves c and d that close-out measures a
non-default atom count. That is safe: SNEK_NUM_ATOMS is deliberately absent from
runner.EVAL_RELEVANT_ENV because a categorical arm's atom count, v_min and v_max are recorded in its own
arch.json and build_eval_agent rebuilds the network from that sidecar, not from the env. BATCH_SIZE and
the target-update knobs are training-only and cannot reach a trained checkpoint at all.

THIS BATCH WAS RESTARTED ONCE, ON PURPOSE. A first version ran one config per arm at a single seed
(n=1), which is below what this project's own noise floor allows; it was killed ~8 minutes in, its data
and its four ledger entries deleted, and re-queued in this shape. A second revision grouped the waves by
SEED rather than by config; that was dropped before launch in favour of this one, because a seed-grouped
wave leaves every config at n=1 until the last wave lands. There is nothing to recover from either.
